table.text: Participants will be recruited from countries where psychedelic use has been decriminalized or legalized in any jurisdiction, pending country-specific approval by the Emory University IRB and international recruitment guidelines; current recruitment includes the United States, Canada, and Australia.
Amendments will be approved by the Emory University IRB, logged on the OSF page, and noted in any publication bearing on affected data.

Ethical approval has been granted by the Emory University Institutional Review Board (#2025P011692).

Participants are recruited into two parallel arms of 800 each: individuals reporting psychedelicrelated challenges and individuals reporting meditation-related challenges, defined as distress or impairment persisting after the acute effects of a psychedelic experience or period of meditation practice have subsided.

Each subsequent component is nested within the preceding one: longitudinal participants are drawn from the cross-sectional sample, and diary participants from the longitudinal sample. presents the study design and timeline.

Invitations to the voice diary component will be issued on a rolling basis to any participant in the psychedelics arm eligible for longitudinal assessment until all n = 40 diary participants are enrolled; these invitations will be made within the first week after baseline completion, with diaries beginning within two weeks of baseline completion.
Participants are then asked to rank the types practiced from most to least, and report cumulative lifetime hours of practice.
In addition, participants are queried about the typical daily meditation schedule they maintained at the time of the precipitating event; and, where a meditation app was used, its name.

Psychedelic-arm participants are asked about psychedelic-specific coping actions (e.g., changing dose or compound, stopping use, reducing or increasing use, or repeating the same psychedelic experience unmodified or modified); meditation-arm participants are asked about contemplative coping strategies (e.g., attention regulation, acceptance or surrender, self-inquiry, reappraisal or application of views, stopping practice, reducing or increasing practice).

In addition, cross-arm use of remedies is assessed: psychedelic-arm participants are asked about contemplative coping strategies for post-psychedelic challenges, and meditation-arm participants are asked about psychedelic use for meditation-related challenges.

At the end of the survey, participants are invited to submit their full account in writing, along with their understanding of why their experience occurred and which responses and remedies they found most and least helpful.

Diary participants are purposely sampled from the longitudinal cohort on the basis of recency and persistence of difficulties: eligible participants report onset of their index experience within the previous six months and ongoing symptoms that are less than 70% resolved.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A sample of n = 800 per arm was selected to support the factor-analytic work described above. Current standards suggest validation samples of at least 300 participants for each stage of exploratory and confirmatory analysis (Clark & Watson, 2019); n = 800 permits splitting each arm into training (n = 400) and testing (n = 400) sets while retaining adequate power in both after attrition. Power analysis for regression models indicates that n = 480 provides greater than 95% power to detect small effects (f² of .2). Additionally, this sample size ensures adequate power to support possible future measure-development work, currently beyond the scope of this protocol.

For the longitudinal component, power was estimated through Monte Carlo simulation (Muthén & Muthén, 2002) using the R package simr, generating 500 samples of n = 240 to account for 40% attrition, with four repeated measures to account for 33% attrition. Models were fitted using lme4 and included time, a longitudinal predictor, their interaction, a level-2 variable with a cross-level interaction, and three additional level-2 covariates, assuming random intercepts. Simulations yielded greater than 95% power to detect an effect of .2.

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.research_questions:
Research Question 1: What kind of lasting meditation or psychedelic-related difficulties are reported across different contexts, in both unrestricted “real world” samples, as well as more “controlled” settings such as clinical trials, religious ceremonies etc.? What is the longitudinal course, duration and impact on functioning of these experiences in these different groups?

      •	Hypothesis 1a: The 59 categories of phenomenology that were catalogued in the Varieties of Contemplative Experience Project (VCE; Lindahl et al., 2017) will be represented in this sample but will be statistically explained by a lesser number of distinct but correlated factors. 

      •	Hypothesis 1b: The duration, severity, and impact on mental health and functioning will range from mild to severe (e.g., > 10-year duration, inability to work, hospitalization, suicidality).

Research Question 2: Given the overlapping phenomenology, benefits, mechanisms and delivery systems of meditation and psychedelics, do the types and course of challenges and adverse effects also overlap? How are they similar or different?  

      •	Hypothesis 2a: Meditation-induced and psychedelic-induced phenomenology will be highly overlapping, with experiences spanning all 7 domains of the VCE codebook (or emergent factors on the Comprehensive Assessment of Meditation-related Challenges (CAMC) or Comprehensive Assessment of Psychedelic-related Challenges (CAPC)). The highest area(s) of overlap will be trauma symptoms (PCL-TRASC; CDS) and sense of self domain (ego-dissolution) items.

      •	Hypothesis 2b: Psychedelic-related AEs will produce more AEs in the perceptual domain (or HPPD factor) than meditation.

      •	Hypothesis 2c: Psychedelic-related AEs will be more severe (greater impairment, duration, intensity) than meditation-related AEs.

Research Question 3: Do the enduring negative effects of meditation or psychedelics resemble any recognized clinical syndromes (e.g., trauma symptoms) that could inform treatment approaches? 

      •	Hypothesis 3a: A subset of adverse effects will resemble dysregulated arousal symptoms that are characteristic of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

      •	Hypothesis 3b: A subset of adverse effects will resemble depersonalization/derealization disorder (DPDR).

      •	Hypothesis 3c: A subset of adverse effects will resemble episodes of hypomania, mania, or psychosis. 

      •	Hypothesis 3d: A subset of adverse effects will resemble obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD).

      •	Hypothesis 3e: A subset of adverse effects will resemble hallucinogen persisting perceptual disorder (HPPD).

Research Question 4. What factors influence the overall trajectories and outcomes? In other words, are there pre-existing factors (person-level demographics, psychiatric or trauma history, type of meditation/ psychedelics, dual-use, dose, set and setting, social support); specific phenomenology (affective, perceptual, cognitive, somatic, sense of self changes), or post-difficulty responses (appraisals, social responses, specific remedies) associated with greater vs. lesser severity, duration and functional impairment?

These include pre-existing factors, phenomenology; and responses:

      •	Pre-existing factors include demographics, health/social history, as well as set, setting and treatment-related factors:

             o	Hypothesis 5a: History of trauma or mental health conditions, marginalized or underprivileged social statuses (e.g., low SES, racial/gender/sexual minorities), and psychosis risk factors (genetic risk, urbanicity etc.) will predict worse outcomes.

             o	Hypothesis 5b: Low scores on the set and setting questionnaire (SSQ) (indicating less prepared (mind)set and less controlled/supportive setting) will correspond to worse outcomes.

             o	Hypothesis 5c Higher dosage of psychedelic and/or meditation practice at time of onset will predict worse outcomes.

      •	Phenomenology-level factors related to the type of challenge or experience:

             o	Hypothesis 5d: Phenomenology related to psychosis (delusions etc.) will predict worse outcomes.

             o	Hypothesis 5e: Decreased sleep (insomnia) and/or eating/appetite will predict worse outcomes.

             o	Hypothesis 5f: Changes in the sense of self domain that are characteristic of depersonalization or loss of basic/minimal self that last > 1 day will predict worse outcomes.
 
             o	Hypothesis 5g: Greater duration of specific phenomenology will predict greater impairment and distress.

      •	Response-level factors assess how participants, as well as the people and systems around them, appraise, interpret and respond to meditation/psychedelic-related challenges adverse effects:

             o	Hypothesis 5h: Higher scores on the institutional betrayal and support questionnaire (IBSQ), indicating lower levels of support and higher levels of betrayal will predict worse outcomes.

             o	Hypothesis 5i: Psychopathological appraisals will be associated with worse outcomes than spiritual appraisals (causal direction undetermined).

Research Question 6. What are helpful and unhelpful responses and remedies for psychedelic and meditation-related challenges? What systems of support already exist, how well do they work, and what needs to be created, modified or expanded to better support individuals undergoing psychedelic or meditation-related challenges? 

      •	Hypotheses: This research question is exploratory.

table.study_design_overview: The study has two parallel arms: a meditation-related challenges arm and a psychedelic-related challenges arm. Recruiting will be conducted separately for each arm and participants will sign up for the study arm that applies to them and for which they qualify. There will be no random assignment.
table.statistical_tests:
Research question 1: Descriptive information about the kinds of meditation and psychedelic-related lasting difficulties will be analyzed both quantitatively and qualitatively. Qualitative analysis will follow the procedures in the VCE study (Lindahl et al., 2017), which utilized the technique of content analysis to create a codebook defining the range of phenomena that participant’s report (Schreier, 2012).  Quantitative analyses will involve reporting descriptive statistics of scales measuring experience phenomenology and impact. 

Research Question 2: Independent sample t tests will be used to investigate whether meditation or psychedelic-related difficulties differ across quantitative measures of their characteristics and longitudinal course. 

Research Question 3: Standard validated measures of identified clinical syndromes will be used to determine whether meditation or psychedelic-related difficulties match or diverge from clinical criteria or symptom patterns for known clinical syndromes (e.g., trauma symptoms, depersonalization, diagnoses measured by the SCL-90R).

Research Question 4: Multiple regression will be used to identify influencing factors (preexisting factors, phenomenology factors, and response factors) that are predictive of the level of duration, impairment, and severity of meditation or psychedelic-related difficulties. Variables for each type of influencing factor (preexisting, phenomenology, response) will be entered into multiple regression models for each outcome. A control variable for study arm (meditation vs. psychedelic) will be added to all regression models. 

Exploratory analyses will also examine whether certain preexisting factors predict symptom phenomenology, and whether certain symptom phenomenology predicts the helpfulness of certain responses/remedies. Exploratory path analyses will be used to examine indirect effects between preexisting factors, phenomenology, responses and outcomes (impairment/duration).

Research Question 5: Qualitative descriptions of remedies will be categorized using content analysis based on participant’s reports of what was most helpful to them. Quantitative endorsements of remedies will be combined with any new categories of remedies stemming from the qualitative data. Next, descriptive statistics will be used to examine participant’s ratings of the effectiveness of each category of remedy.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Participants who do not pass data quality checks will be excluded from data. These include attention check questions throughout survey (e.g., “Please select “Moderately” for intensity and "1 day or less" for duration to show you are paying attention to this question”) and any response other than “Yes I will” to the following question: “Do you commit to providing thoughtful answers to the questions in this survey?” Finally, entries with qualitative responses that are clearly indicative of poor-quality data (i.e., repetitive, non-sensical) will be excluded. 

All variables that are used in inferential statistics will be examined for extreme outliers, as defined by the interquartile range (values outside of Q1 - 3 * IQR or Q3 + 3 * IQR). Such values will be winsorized by substituting extreme values with the minimum or maximum score within this specified interquartile range.
table.sample_size: This study aims to collect a sample of between 300 and 3000 participants (150-1500 for each study arm). These numbers were determined by conducting power analyses to determine minimum and maximum sample size requirements for the quantitative analyses (analyses for research questions 2 and 4). If recruitment does not reach the goal of a minimum of 300 participants within the allotted timeframe (2 years of recruitment), then analyses will be conducted on the available sample size. The success of the project is not contingent on sample size. Research questions 1, 3 and 5 are exploratory and descriptive and will be answered regardless of final sample size. Analyses for research question 4 (influencing factors) may be adjusted for a smaller sample size.
table.additional_comments:
LIST OF MEASURES:

SURVEY SECTION 1:
MEDITATION/ PSYCHEDELIC USE HISTORY
Psychedelic/meditation use history include the type(s) and amount of lifetime meditation/psychedelic use, the agent(s) that triggered the difficulty; and meditation-psychedelic dual use.

SURVEY SECTION 2: 
PRE-EXISTING INFLUENCING FACTORS
 Pre-Existing person-level factors
      •	Demographics
             o	Age 
             o	Left/right handedness 
             o	Country of birth/Country of current residence 
             o	Gender 
             o	Race/Ethnicity/Minoritized status in current country 
             o	Sexual Orientation 
             o	Religious affiliation & observance 
             o	Education 
             o	Socioeconomic Status 
      •	Mental health history checklist: This check list assesses the presence of personal and/or family psychiatric illness and trauma history. These factors have been found to be distal risk factors for developing meditation/psychedelic-related adverse effects. 
      •	Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE; Felitti et al., 1998): Childhood adversity is a commonly recognized risk factor that contributes to vulnerability across a range of mental and physical health domains. It is therefore an important individual difference to assess in meditation/psychedelic-related adverse experiences. 
      •	Set and Setting questionnaire (under development, see measure development methods section for item sources): These questions ask about contextual factors present at the time of onset, or when meditation/psychedelic-related adverse effects first started. Agent questions include type, dose and prior experience with meditation/psychedelic. “Setting” questions include preparatory behaviors, location, social context, quality of support of guidance and additional supports. “Set” questions ask about participants mental/physical health, intentions and mindset at the time of onset of meditation/psychedelic-related difficulties. These set and setting variables have been found or hypothesized to be proximal risk factors for developing meditation/psychedelic related adverse effects and their severity. 

SURVEY SECTION 3:
MEDITATION OR PSYCHEDELIC-RELATED CHALLENGES (PHENOMENOLOGY)

The following measures were included as part of the item-pool for development of the Comprehensive Assessment of Meditation/Psychedelic-related Challenges (CAMC/CAPC-372). Furthermore, validated questionnaires were included in their entirety in order to compare and contrast meditation/psychedelic-related adverse effects with known clinical syndromes (e.g., PTSD, DPDR), and/or constructs that have been used in prior research (e.g., mystical experience). 
      •	Meditation/Psychedelic-Related Adverse Effects Scale (MRAES/PRAES; Britton, 2018; Simonsson et al., 2023): This questionnaire consists of 11 items, which query specific meditation-related adverse effects that have been derived based on prior research. It is a check-list of known adverse effects and the rationale for including it in this study is to identify which of these effects are being experienced by current participants, and to establish correspondence of these known types of adverse effects with other standardized measures. 
      •	Symptom Checklist-90 (SCL-90; Derogatis, 1992): This questionnaire assesses 9 domains of clinically relevant symptoms (e.g., anxiety), as well as global functioning indices. The rationale for this measure is to establish a standardized assessment of a variety of standardized mental health symptoms that individuals might experience in association with meditation/psychedelic -related adverse effects. 
      •	Metacognitive Process of Decentering Scale, Short Form (Hanley et al., 2020): This questionnaire assesses participant propensity toward Decentering, a documented metacognitive effect of meditation and psychedelic use whereby one recognizes a distinction between oneself and one’s thoughts. There is overlap between decentering and certain components of dissociative experiences, making this an important construct to measure when assessing varied responses to meditation. 
      •	Cambridge Depersonalization Scale (CDS; Sierra & Berrios, 2000): Depersonalization, a type of dissociation, was previously reported in qualitative research about meditation/psychedelic--related adverse effects, and is a plausible correlate of meditation/psychedelic related adverse effects since many meditation techniques and psychedelic communities focus on changing one’s relationship to one’s self- concept. Therefore, the Cambridge Depersonalization Scale will be used to assess depersonalization in a standardized way. 
      •	The Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ-30; Barrett et al., 2015): this questionnaire measures a construct that includes changes to the sense of self, changes in perception of time and space, feelings of ineffability, spiritual appraisals, and positive emotion. Many of these characteristics are found in both meditation and psychedelic use and have been found to be predictors of clinical outcomes. 
      •	HPPD Questionnaire (Locke, 2022): Hallucinogen Persistent Perceptual Disorder is a DSM-5 diagnosis characterized by the reexperiencing of certain perceptual symptoms after the use of a psychedelic substance. This questionnaire assesses common perceptual symptoms of this disorder and is included due to the similarities of these symptoms with qualitative descriptions of meditation-related adverse effects. 
      •	Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist, Trauma-Related Altered States of Consciousness (PCL-TRASC; Frewen et al., 2017): The experience of meditation/psychedelic-related adverse effects may be traumatic. Altered states of consciousness have been reported in association with meditation/psychedelic-related adverse effects specifically, and may be associated with trauma symptoms more broadly. For this reason, we will use the PCL-TRASC to assess trauma-related altered states (e.g., dissociation) in particular, as they may arise as a result of meditation/psychedelic- related adverse effects. 
      •	Religious and Spiritual Struggle Scale (Exline et al., 2014): Individuals often practice meditation or take psychedelics as part of a religious or spiritual framework. When they experience adverse effects, this may contribute to religious or spiritual struggle which, in turn, may exacerbate other challenges. 
      •	Selected items or subscales were also used from the following questionnaires:
      •	The Psychotomimetic States Inventory (PSI; Mason et al., 2008) is a measure of psychotic-like acute subjective drug effects. The cognitive disorganization, delusional thinking, mania, and perceptual distortion subscales were included in the present research in order to capture changes in executive functioning, cognition, delusional thinking, affective lability, and perception that were described through previous qualitative research on meditation-related challenges (Lindahl et al., 2017) but were not sufficiently captured by other questionnaires. 
      •	The Altered States of Consciousness Rating Scale (AOV; Studerus et al., 2010) is a measure of altered states of consciousness that has been extensively used in research on psychedelic-related subjective experiences. The most recent version of the scale includes 11 subscales, 5 of which were included in the present research: impaired control and cognition, elementary imagery, complex imagery, changed meaning of percepts, and audio-visual synesthesia. These subscales were included to measure changes in executive functioning, loss of agency, and visual imagery that were not sufficiently captured by other questionnaires yet were described in previous qualitative research on meditation-related challenges (Lindahl et al., 2017).
      •	The Self and Self-Boundary Loss Characteristics Scale (Canby et al., in preparation): is a measure of changes to one’s sense of self and/or the diminishment of the boundaries between self and objects, other people, and/or the world. The present research includes subscales measuring a sense of unity with all things, boundary diminishment with others, boundary diminishment with objects, loss of self, and loss of the sense of ownership of thoughts and feelings. These experiences have been described previously in the context of meditation-related challenges (Lindahl & Britton, 2019) and are thus important to include in the present research. 
      •	The Inventory of Non-Ordinary Experiences (INOE; Taves et al., 2023) is a measure of experiences that may be considered religious, mystical, psychopathological, or anomalous. It is designed to measure the interaction of mind and culture and thus does not make assumptions about how these experiences are interpreted. Items measuring unusual experiences that were not captured by other questionnaires (e.g., lucid dreaming, paralysis, possession experiences) were included in the present research in order to measure a comprehensive range of experiences. 
      •	The Challenging Experiences Questionnaire (CEQ; Barrett et al., 2016): is a measure of acute challenging psychedelic experiences. Items measuring specific fears of losing one’s mind and experiencing one’s own death were included due to a lack of coverage of these topics from other questionnaires.
      •	The Thalbourne Kundalini Scale (TKS; Thalbourne, 1999) is a measure of the energy-like psychophysiological phenomena that has been termed “kundalini.” Selected items were included from the scale measuring involuntary movements, somatic energy-like sensations, and thermal changes when these phenomena were not captured by other scales. 

SURVEY SECTION 4: 
POST-DIFFICULTY INFLUENCING RESPONSES AND REMEDIES
4.1 Appraisals Frameworks and Explanations: This section asks about how participants interpret or make sense of their experience. Participants are asked whether they have encountered various interpretive frameworks to make sense of their meditation or psychedelic-related difficulties and the degree to which each of these frameworks were helpful or harmful. Participants are asked about encountering both spiritual/religious frameworks and scientific/biological/trauma-related frameworks. 
4.2 Social Responses: 
      •	Social Reactions Questionnaire-Shortened (SRQ-S; Ullman et al., 2017): This is a 16-item measure assessing different kinds of responses to the disclosure of meditation-related adverse effects. Previous research has found that the ways in which others respond to self-disclosures about harmful effects experienced within established social institutions can have important influence on persons’ recovery from harmful events. However, little is known about how these kinds of responses influence recovery from meditation-related adverse effects. This questionnaire will help identify types of social responses as a determinant of outcomes and severity of meditation related adverse effects. 
      •	Institutional Betrayal and Support Questionnaire (Rosenthal et al., 2016): Like the Social Responses Questionnaire, this scale assesses different kinds of responses to disclosure of meditation-related adverse effects. This scale is more extensive, and also more tailored to the ways in which institutions respond to harms that happen under their purview. Responses to this scale can help to identify systemic and structural determinants of differences in the course and outcome of meditation-related adverse effects. 
4.3 Remedies. In response to focus group recommendations to provide solutions along with problems, this study aims to provide information about what types of remedies or treatments are most and least helpful for enduring psychedelic difficulties. Participants provide both free responses as well as ratings of therapies, medications, alternative medicine treatments and/or integration support services that they tried, so that any information about negative effects will be paired with evidence-based information about available solutions.
SURVEY SECTION 5:
IMPACT AND OUTCOMES
      •	Impacts checklist assesses various types of impacts that may result due to meditation/psychedelic-related adverse effects, including inpatient hospitalization, urgent care/emergency room visit; suicide attempt or self-harm, psychotropic medication, outpatient services, and involvement of law enforcement.
      •	World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS; Ustun, 2012): This is a standardized measure of functional impairment that can help to identify areas of impairment that are comparable to impairment from other causes. 
      •	The Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Scale - Global Health (PROMIS-GH; Elsman et al., 2021): this is a brief assessment of global health and functioning, which is typically used to assess whole health and wellbeing including psychological, physical, and relational aspects of health. As an index of general health, this measure is important for understanding and interpreting the general impacts of meditation-related adverse effects on individuals’ wellbeing. 
QUALITATIVE SECTION:

In addition to the survey, participants will be asked the following free-response questions:

    1.	What is your understanding of why your meditation/psychedelic-related difficulties occurred what caused them? 
    2.	In your own words, please describe what has been most helpful for you. 
    3.	In your own words, please describe what has been most unhelpful or even harmful for you. 
    4.	Please tell us your story, in whatever form you choose, including whatever information you think is most important to include. There is no word limit, but we suggest keeping it under 3000 words. Submitting a story is optional.

SURVEY SECTION 1:
MEDITATION/ PSYCHEDELIC USE HISTORY
Psychedelic/meditation use history include the type(s) and amount of lifetime meditation/psychedelic use, the agent(s) that triggered the difficulty; and meditation-psychedelic dual use.

SURVEY SECTION 2:
PRE-EXISTING INFLUENCING FACTORS
Pre-Existing person-level factors
•\tDemographics
o\tAge
o\tLeft/right handedness
o\tCountry of birth/Country of current residence
o\tGender
o\tRace/Ethnicity/Minoritized status in current country
o\tSexual Orientation
o\tReligious affiliation & observance
o\tEducation
o\tSocioeconomic Status
•\tMental health history checklist: This check list assesses the presence of personal and/or family psychiatric illness and trauma history. These factors have been found to be distal risk factors for developing meditation/psychedelic-related adverse effects.
•\tAdverse Childhood Experiences (ACE; Felitti et al., 1998): Childhood adversity is a commonly recognized risk factor that contributes to vulnerability across a range of mental and physical health domains. It is therefore an important individual difference to assess in meditation/psychedelic-related adverse experiences.
•\tSet and Setting questionnaire (under development, see measure development methods section for item sources): These questions ask about contextual factors present at the time of onset, or when meditation/psychedelic-related adverse effects first started. Agent questions include type, dose and prior experience with meditation/psychedelic. “Setting” questions include preparatory behaviors, location, social context, quality of support of guidance and additional supports. “Set” questions ask about participants mental/physical health, intentions and mindset at the time of onset of meditation/psychedelic-related difficulties. These set and setting variables have been found or hypothesized to be proximal risk factors for developing meditation/psychedelic related adverse effects and their severity.

SURVEY SECTION 3:
MEDITATION OR PSYCHEDELIC-RELATED CHALLENGES (PHENOMENOLOGY)

The following measures were included as part of the item-pool for development of the Comprehensive Assessment of Meditation/Psychedelic-related Challenges (CAMC/CAPC-372). Furthermore, validated questionnaires were included in their entirety in order to compare and contrast meditation/psychedelic-related adverse effects with known clinical syndromes (e.g., PTSD, DPDR), and/or constructs that have been used in prior research (e.g., mystical experience).
•\tMeditation/Psychedelic-Related Adverse Effects Scale (MRAES/PRAES; Britton, 2018; Simonsson et al., 2023): This questionnaire consists of 11 items, which query specific meditation-related adverse effects that have been derived based on prior research. It is a check-list of known adverse effects and the rationale for including it in this study is to identify which of these effects are being experienced by current participants, and to establish correspondence of these known types of adverse effects with other standardized measures.
•\tSymptom Checklist-90 (SCL-90; Derogatis, 1992): This questionnaire assesses 9 domains of clinically relevant symptoms (e.g., anxiety), as well as global functioning indices. The rationale for this measure is to establish a standardized assessment of a variety of standardized mental health symptoms that individuals might experience in association with meditation/psychedelic -related adverse effects.
•\tMetacognitive Process of Decentering Scale, Short Form (Hanley et al., 2020): This questionnaire assesses participant propensity toward Decentering, a documented metacognitive effect of meditation and psychedelic use whereby one recognizes a distinction between oneself and one’s thoughts. There is overlap between decentering and certain components of dissociative experiences, making this an important construct to measure when assessing varied responses to meditation.
•\tCambridge Depersonalization Scale (CDS; Sierra & Berrios, 2000): Depersonalization, a type of dissociation, was previously reported in qualitative research about meditation/psychedelic--related adverse effects, and is a plausible correlate of meditation/psychedelic related adverse effects since many meditation techniques and psychedelic communities focus on changing one’s relationship to one’s self- concept. Therefore, the Cambridge Depersonalization Scale will be used to assess depersonalization in a standardized way.
•\tThe Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ-30; Barrett et al., 2015): this questionnaire measures a construct that includes changes to the sense of self, changes in perception of time and space, feelings of ineffability, spiritual appraisals, and positive emotion. Many of these characteristics are found in both meditation and psychedelic use and have been found to be predictors of clinical outcomes.
•\tHPPD Questionnaire (Locke, 2022): Hallucinogen Persistent Perceptual Disorder is a DSM-5 diagnosis characterized by the reexperiencing of certain perceptual symptoms after the use of a psychedelic substance. This questionnaire assesses common perceptual symptoms of this disorder and is included due to the similarities of these symptoms with qualitative descriptions of meditation-related adverse effects.
•\tPost-Traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist, Trauma-Related Altered States of Consciousness (PCL-TRASC; Frewen et al., 2017): The experience of meditation/psychedelic-related adverse effects may be traumatic. Altered states of consciousness have been reported in association with meditation/psychedelic-related adverse effects specifically, and may be associated with trauma symptoms more broadly. For this reason, we will use the PCL-TRASC to assess trauma-related altered states (e.g., dissociation) in particular, as they may arise as a result of meditation/psychedelic- related adverse effects.
•\tReligious and Spiritual Struggle Scale (Exline et al., 2014): Individuals often practice meditation or take psychedelics as part of a religious or spiritual framework. When they experience adverse effects, this may contribute to religious or spiritual struggle which, in turn, may exacerbate other challenges.
•\tSelected items or subscales were also used from the following questionnaires:
•\tThe Psychotomimetic States Inventory (PSI; Mason et al., 2008) is a measure of psychotic-like acute subjective drug effects. The cognitive disorganization, delusional thinking, mania, and perceptual distortion subscales were included in the present research in order to capture changes in executive functioning, cognition, delusional thinking, affective lability, and perception that were described through previous qualitative research on meditation-related challenges (Lindahl et al., 2017) but were not sufficiently captured by other questionnaires.
•\tThe Altered States of Consciousness Rating Scale (AOV; Studerus et al., 2010) is a measure of altered states of consciousness that has been extensively used in research on psychedelic-related subjective experiences. The most recent version of the scale includes 11 subscales, 5 of which were included in the present research: impaired control and cognition, elementary imagery, complex imagery, changed meaning of percepts, and audio-visual synesthesia. These subscales were included to measure changes in executive functioning, loss of agency, and visual imagery that were not sufficiently captured by other questionnaires yet were described in previous qualitative research on meditation-related challenges (Lindahl et al., 2017).
•\tThe Self and Self-Boundary Loss Characteristics Scale (Canby et al., in preparation): is a measure of changes to one’s sense of self and/or the diminishment of the boundaries between self and objects, other people, and/or the world. The present research includes subscales measuring a sense of unity with all things, boundary diminishment with others, boundary diminishment with objects, loss of self, and loss of the sense of ownership of thoughts and feelings. These experiences have been described previously in the context of meditation-related challenges (Lindahl & Britton, 2019) and are thus important to include in the present research.
•\tThe Inventory of Non-Ordinary Experiences (INOE; Taves et al., 2023) is a measure of experiences that may be considered religious, mystical, psychopathological, or anomalous. It is designed to measure the interaction of mind and culture and thus does not make assumptions about how these experiences are interpreted. Items measuring unusual experiences that were not captured by other questionnaires (e.g., lucid dreaming, paralysis, possession experiences) were included in the present research in order to measure a comprehensive range of experiences.
•\tThe Challenging Experiences Questionnaire (CEQ; Barrett et al., 2016): is a measure of acute challenging psychedelic experiences. Items measuring specific fears of losing one’s mind and experiencing one’s own death were included due to a lack of coverage of these topics from other questionnaires.
•\tThe Thalbourne Kundalini Scale (TKS; Thalbourne, 1999) is a measure of the energy-like psychophysiological phenomena that has been termed “kundalini.” Selected items were included from the scale measuring involuntary movements, somatic energy-like sensations, and thermal changes when these phenomena were not captured by other scales.

SURVEY SECTION 4:
POST-DIFFICULTY INFLUENCING RESPONSES AND REMEDIES
4.1 Appraisals Frameworks and Explanations: This section asks about how participants interpret or make sense of their experience. Participants are asked whether they have encountered various interpretive frameworks to make sense of their meditation or psychedelic-related difficulties and the degree to which each of these frameworks were helpful or harmful. Participants are asked about encountering both spiritual/religious frameworks and scientific/biological/trauma-related frameworks.
4.2 Social Responses:
•\tSocial Reactions Questionnaire-Shortened (SRQ-S; Ullman et al., 2017): This is a 16-item measure assessing different kinds of responses to the disclosure of meditation-related adverse effects. Previous research has found that the ways in which others respond to self-disclosures about harmful effects experienced within established social institutions can have important influence on persons’ recovery from harmful events. However, little is known about how these kinds of responses influence recovery from meditation-related adverse effects. This questionnaire will help identify types of social responses as a determinant of outcomes and severity of meditation related adverse effects.
•\tInstitutional Betrayal and Support Questionnaire (Rosenthal et al., 2016): Like the Social Responses Questionnaire, this scale assesses different kinds of responses to disclosure of meditation-related adverse effects. This scale is more extensive, and also more tailored to the ways in which institutions respond to harms that happen under their purview. Responses to this scale can help to identify systemic and structural determinants of differences in the course and outcome of meditation-related adverse effects.
4.3 Remedies. In response to focus group recommendations to provide solutions along with problems, this study aims to provide information about what types of remedies or treatments are most and least helpful for enduring psychedelic difficulties. Participants provide both free responses as well as ratings of therapies, medications, alternative medicine treatments and/or integration support services that they tried, so that any information about negative effects will be paired with evidence-based information about available solutions.
SURVEY SECTION 5:
IMPACT AND OUTCOMES
•\tImpacts checklist assesses various types of impacts that may result due to meditation/psychedelic-related adverse effects, including inpatient hospitalization, urgent care/emergency room visit; suicide attempt or self-harm, psychotropic medication, outpatient services, and involvement of law enforcement.
•\tWorld Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS; Ustun, 2012): This is a standardized measure of functional impairment that can help to identify areas of impairment that are comparable to impairment from other causes.
•\tThe Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Scale - Global Health (PROMIS-GH; Elsman et al., 2021): this is a brief assessment of global health and functioning, which is typically used to assess whole health and wellbeing including psychological, physical, and relational aspects of health. As an index of general health, this measure is important for understanding and interpreting the general impacts of meditation-related adverse effects on individuals’ wellbeing.
QUALITATIVE SECTION:

In addition to the survey, participants will be asked the following free-response questions:

1.\tWhat is your understanding of why your meditation/psychedelic-related difficulties occurred what caused them?
2.\tIn your own words, please describe what has been most helpful for you.
3.\tIn your own words, please describe what has been most unhelpful or even harmful for you.
4.\tPlease tell us your story, in whatever form you choose, including whatever information you think is most important to include. There is no word limit, but we suggest keeping it under 3000 words. Submitting a story is optional.

live_data_statements: Participants are recruited into two parallel arms of 800 each: individuals reporting psychedelicrelated challenges and individuals reporting meditation-related challenges, defined as distress or impairment persisting after the acute effects of a psychedelic experience or period of meditation practice have subsided.

Each subsequent component is nested within the preceding one: longitudinal participants are drawn from the cross-sectional sample, and diary participants from the longitudinal sample. presents the study design and timeline.

Invitations to the voice diary component will be issued on a rolling basis to any participant in the psychedelics arm eligible for longitudinal assessment until all n = 40 diary participants are enrolled; these invitations will be made within the first week after baseline completion, with diaries beginning within two weeks of baseline completion.
Participants are then asked to rank the types practiced from most to least, and report cumulative lifetime hours of practice.
In addition, participants are queried about the typical daily meditation schedule they maintained at the time of the precipitating event; and, where a meditation app was used, its name.

Psychedelic-arm participants are asked about psychedelic-specific coping actions (e.g., changing dose or compound, stopping use, reducing or increasing use, or repeating the same psychedelic experience unmodified or modified); meditation-arm participants are asked about contemplative coping strategies (e.g., attention regulation, acceptance or surrender, self-inquiry, reappraisal or application of views, stopping practice, reducing or increasing practice).

In addition, cross-arm use of remedies is assessed: psychedelic-arm participants are asked about contemplative coping strategies for post-psychedelic challenges, and meditation-arm participants are asked about psychedelic use for meditation-related challenges.

At the end of the survey, participants are invited to submit their full account in writing, along with their understanding of why their experience occurred and which responses and remedies they found most and least helpful.

Diary participants are purposely sampled from the longitudinal cohort on the basis of recency and persistence of difficulties: eligible participants report onset of their index experience within the previous six months and ongoing symptoms that are less than 70% resolved.
Consistent with prior work using naturalistic narrative speech prompts (Kaplan et al., 2025), participants are instructed to "try to talk about this in a stream-of-conscious way for about 5 minutes.
Participants are invited to take breaks and resume at their convenience, and those who do not complete are contacted up to three times to identify barriers and provide reminders.
The second is the observational design: participants are not randomized, precluding causal inference.
Participants are clearly informed of study expectations, encouraged to commit to completion, and supported through reminders and follow-ups led by dedicated study personnel.

Because the study involves reporting the use of substances that are currently illegal in several countries, the requirement for written documentation of consent has been waived, on the grounds that a signed consent document would constitute the principal record linking participants to the study and would therefore represent the primary risk of breach of confidentiality.

text.text: Introduction: Psychedelics and meditation are increasingly used for therapeutic and wellness purposes.

However, research into adverse effects (AEs) has been limited, without adequate investigation of the nature, clinical characteristics, and diversity of persisting challenges following psychedelic use and meditation practice.

This study aims to better characterize the clinical and contextual features of these challenges, describe their longitudinal course, and compare psychedelic-related challenges to meditation-related challenges, selected as comparator conditions given previously characterized phenomenological and contextual overlap between the two.

This is a mixed-methods, enriched-sample, active-comparator (psychedelics vs. meditation) observational study comprising (1) a cross-sectional retrospective survey (N = 1,600), (2) a prospective 12-month longitudinal design involving six bimonthly surveys (n = 800), (3) 12 weeks of weekly ambulatory assessments combining quantitative symptom ratings with narrative voice report (n = 40), and (4) qualitative interviews (n = 60).

Participants are recruited into two parallel arms of 800 each: individuals reporting psychedelicrelated challenges and individuals reporting meditation-related challenges, defined as distress or impairment persisting after the acute effects of a psychedelic experience or period of meditation practice have subsided.

Data collection includes a tailored item pool aimed at capturing the symptoms and phenomenology of these challenges in detail, developed from qualitative research and collaboratively with stakeholders with lived experience.

The World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS 2.0) and measures of agent/exposure, set, setting, and social response are administered to characterize biopsychosocial correlates and functional impacts of AEs.

Initial analyses will describe the phenomenology, course, and functional impact of psychedelic-and meditation-related challenges, and evaluate the structure and psychometric properties of the novel item pool.

The study will produce a publicly available de-identified dataset supporting subsequent analyses, such as correspondence with recognized clinical syndromes, trajectory characterization, and cross-arm comparison of measurement structure, reported in registered reports or preregistrations.
This protocol describes an observational, active-comparator naturalistic study of psychedelic-related and meditation-related adverse effects (AEs).

Psychedelics and meditation have both shown evidence of efficacy for addressing multiple difficult-to-treat psychiatric symptoms in clinical populations and for enhancing wellbeing in adults (Griffiths et al., 2016; Goldberg et al., 2022; Hoge et al., 2023; Mitchell et al., 2021; Raison et al., 2023).

text.text: Characterizing unexpected and unwanted effects in psychedelics and meditation is complicated by the fact that both practices can produce intense, difficult, or disorienting experiences during the acute period, many of which resolve without lasting consequence.
This protocol therefore focuses on effects with persistent or lasting impact.

Throughout this protocol we use adverse effect (AE) to denote distress or functional impairment that persists after the acute effects of a psychedelic experience or a period of meditation practice have subsided: challenging, difficult, or distressing sequelae that impact everyday functioning (Britton et al., 2021; Ward et al., 2026).

Among individuals with a history of psychedelic use across naturalistic contexts-including recreational, ceremonial, and therapeutic use outside of clinical trials-an estimated 6.4-8.9% report difficulties or functional impairment persisting beyond one day (Simonsson et al., 2023; Olofsson et al., 2026), and 1.3% report difficulties lasting more than a year (Olofsson et al., 2026).

text.text: The remainder of this introduction develops the rationale for the study's design: the state of research into psychedelic-and meditation-related difficulties, measurement gaps present in both fields, and the logic of using meditation-related challenges as a comparator condition for post-psychedelic challenges, before stating the study's research questions.
A discussion of the state of research in both of these respective areas-as well as their outstanding needs-follows below.

Classic psychedelics, including psilocybin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), dimethyltryptamine (DMT), and related serotonergic compounds, produce marked, temporary alterations in perception, cognition, and sense of self, and have been investigated as adjuncts to psychotherapy for depression, post-traumatic stress, and substance use disorders (Griffiths et al., 2016; Mitchell et al., 2021; Goodwin et al., 2022).

text.text: Although they remain Schedule I controlled substances in the United States, several have received FDA breakthrough-therapy designation, are the subject of active Investigational New Drug applications, and their use in the general population has grown substantially in recent years (RAND, 2026).

text.text: As interest in therapeutic potential and general public use grow in parallel, so do the stakes for a rigorous characterization of the harms that can follow these experiences.
Evidence of such potential for harm has accumulated alongside the evidence of benefit (Breeksema et al., 2022; Simonsson et al., 2023), but its measurement remains uneven.

text.text: The assessment of acutely challenging experiences during psychedelic sessions is comparatively well-established (Barrett et al., 2016); the assessment of post-psychedelic difficulties, however, remains underdeveloped in two respects.

text.text: A recent systematic review found that under 25% of psychedelic clinical trials conducted since 2006 used any systematic AE reporting.

Furthermore, adverse events in clinical trials have typically been captured through standardized medicalcoding frameworks such as MedDRA (Brown et al., 1999), which were developed for conventional drug trials and are poorly suited to describing phenomena that psychedelics may produce, such as subjective and perceptual disturbances, disruptions to the sense of self, and interpersonal or psychotherapeutic sequelae (Palitsky et al., 2024a), and may therefore miss the effects of greatest clinical relevance.

text.text: Moreover, much of what is known about enduring difficulties outside of clinical trials is based on retrospective self-reports without repeated longitudinal follow-up, such that inference is limited by recall bias and the absence of documentation regarding the timing and context of onset (Shiffman, Stone, & Hufford, 2008).

text.text: Meditation has yielded a more developed, albeit still limited, literature on AEs.
Meditation here refers to a broad family of contemplative practices that train attention, cognition, affect, and self-related processing.

Rather than adopting a tradition-specific definition, we characterize meditation in mechanistic terms following Dahl, Lutz, and Davidson (2015), who distinguish attentional, constructive, and deconstructive families of practice, and Dorjee (2016), who frames contemplative practice in terms of the mind's metacognitive self-regulatory capacity and associated modes of existential awareness.

text.text: This mixed-methods investigation identified 59 experiential categories of meditation-related challenge across affective, cognitive, perceptual, somatic, conative, social, and sense-of-self domains.

Historically, most quantitative meditation research has assessed adverse experiences using single items or narrow negative-affect indices rather than instruments designed to capture the full range of reported phenomena (Van Dam et al., 2025).

text.text: Where harms have been monitored in trials at all, monitoring has been inconsistent and adverse-event reporting correspondingly sparse: A systematic review of mindfulness-based stress reduction and cognitive therapy trials found that only a small proportion of eligible RCTs reported monitoring for adverse events at all, and that reported adverse-event rates in those that did were under 1% (Wong et al., 2018).

text.text: A growing body of multi-item and phenomenological work has begun to address this gap (Britton et al. 2021; Goldberg et al., 2022; Schlosser, 2019; Van Dam et al., 2025), but the evidence base remains small, and prospective data on the emergence and resolution of these difficulties are scarcer.

text.text: Meditation-related AEs overlap with psychedelic-related AEs in both phenomenological and contextual characteristics, which is what makes meditation the most informative available comparator condition (Grob & Grigsby, 2022; Millière et al., 2018; Palitsky et al., 2024b).

text.text: What has not been established systematically and empirically is the precise nature of this overlap: where these challenges converge in their features, course, and impact, and where they diverge.
The present study's parallel, enriched-sample design is built to answer these questions.

Considered together, these two literatures are characterized by a number of common deficits, described in a recent integrative review (Palitsky et al., 2024b), which proposes an agenda for advancing AE research in both domains.

text.text: Specifically, AE measurement strategies require improvements in detail and comprehensiveness, grounding in the experiences of affected individuals, orientation to real-world impact, standardization, and representativeness.

To help address some of these needs, this project aims to improve the content validity (i.e., comprehensiveness, relation to phenomenology, grounding in stakeholder experiences) and advance the methodological rigor of AE assessment related to meditation and psychedelics use.

This study offers considerable granularity in assessing the range of phenomenology that AEs related to these practices may produce, including dissociation, perceptual changes, somatic disturbances, and existential distress-above and beyond the narrow set of general symptoms such as anxiety or depressed mood.

It remains unclear whether meditation-related and postpsychedelic challenges constitute variants of recognized clinical syndromes, on one hand, or phenomena not captured by existing nosology, on the other.

The assessment approach described in this protocol embeds established measures of clinical symptoms, including depression, anxiety, dissociation, somatic symptoms, alongside novel, phenomenologically-oriented items.
This design enables future benchmarking of psychedelic-and meditation-related challenges against recognized syndromes in pre-registered analyses.
There is also a need for chronological assessment beyond cross-sectional self-report, in AE research related to meditation and psychedelics.
Longitudinal research methods make it possible to prospectively assess the course, duration, and persistence of these challenges, as well as longitudinal predictors of improvement and worsening.
Addressing this lacuna is a central rationale for the longitudinal component of the present design.

This protocol describes a mixed-methods, enriched-sample observational study of psychedelic-related and meditation-related challenges, comprising parallel cross-sectional, longitudinal, qualitative interview, and intensive weekly mixed-method diary components (described in Materials and Methods).

Notably, several of the symptom batteries and set-andsetting measures were co-developed with stakeholders with lived experience of these challenges and grounded in existing research characterizing AEs (Sánchez et al., 2021; Boness et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Notably, several of the symptom batteries and set-andsetting measures were co-developed with stakeholders with lived experience of these challenges and grounded in existing research characterizing AEs <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Sánchez et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Boness et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The study is designed to yield a uniquely detailed dataset characterizing these challenges and their impacts, and to serve as a foundation for a pre-registered program of subsequent analyses.
Three sets of research questions guide the initial analyses planned for this study.
The first of these is: What are the phenomenological features of psychedelic-and meditation-related challenges, and what is the structure of these features?

Initial analyses will describe the Comprehensive Assessment of Psychedelic-related Challenges (CAPC; see below for description) and Comprehensive Assessment of Meditation-related Challenges (CAMC; see below for description) batteries and evaluate their structure and psychometric properties using exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis.

The second set of questions is: How are these challenges experienced by those affected, what are their impacts on day-to-day life, how do these impacts unfold over time, and to what extent are they associated with functional impairment?

These questions are addressed through qualitative interviews, weekly mixed-method diaries collected via a smartphone-administered ecological momentary assessments using Fabla (Kaplan et al., 2025), and the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS 2.0; Üstün et al., 2010).

text.text: The third set of questions is: To what extent do psychedelic-related and meditationrelated challenges converge or diverge in their features, course, and impacts?
The parallel twoarm design permits direct descriptive comparison across all study components.
Additional questions related to this research program will be addressed in pre-registered analyses and registered reports (see Open Science strategy).
Beyond these initial and planned analyses, a central aim of this study is to establish a publicly available anonymized dataset intended to serve as a resource for the field.

The breadth of assessment described here supports a variety of research questions concerning meditation-and psychedelic-related AEs, their contexts, and impacts The dataset and associated materials will be made available to researchers (see Open Science Strategy).
This is a two-armed (psychedelics and meditation) mixed-methods observational study.

It comprises a cross-sectional retrospective online surveys (n = 800 per arm; N = 1,600), which serve as the baseline for longitudinal follow-ups among a subset of participants with current unresolved symptoms from recent-onset AEs (n = 400 per arm; N = 800), consisting of six bimonthly surveys over 12 months.

Qualitative interviews will be conducted with a subsample of participants (n = 30 per arm; N = 60), and an additional subset of n = 40 participants drawn from the longitudinal sample will be invited to complete weekly ambulatory assessments comprising quantitative symptom ratings and a narrative voice diary for 12 weeks.

Each subsequent component is nested within the preceding one: longitudinal participants are drawn from the cross-sectional sample, and diary participants from the longitudinal sample. presents the study design and timeline.
An enriched-sample design was chosen to support detailed characterization of these challenges.

General-population cohort studies can estimate how frequently such difficulties occur, but at realistic incidence rates they yield too few affected individuals to characterize the structure of those difficulties in depth: a cohort of several hundred beginning meditators produces on the order of dozens of adverse-effect cases (Ward et al., 2026), insufficient for detailed analyses of phenomenology or quantitative approaches that can identify symptom clustering.

text.text: Solely recruiting individuals who have already experienced psychedelic-or meditation-related challenges concentrates the sample on the phenomena of interest and permits the detailed, multi-method assessment described below, although it forecloses analyses of prevalence of these AEs in the general populations of meditators or psychedelics takers.

All components of the study will be conducted online, with surveys delivered via the Qualtrics survey platform, interviews conducted over the Zoom teleconferencing platform, and weekly assessments collected via the Fabla app (Kaplan et al., 2025).

text.text: This research will recruit N = 1,600 participants into two equal study arms (n = 800 each), identified by primary precipitating exposure (psychedelics vs. meditation).

Inclusion in either arm requires an experience the participant believes was caused by the psychedelic use or meditation practice, and which persisted after the acute effects of the substance had subsided or beyond a single meditation session, and either (1) caused distress, (2) negatively impacted the participant's life or functioning, or (3) required additional support or treatment.
The definition is common to both arms, differing only in the precipitating event.

Psychedelic-arm AEs must be precipitated by either a "classical" psychedelic (5-HT2A receptor agonist), such as LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca, DMT, 5-MeO-DMT, or mescaline, or by compounds that have been culturally classed with psychedelics, such as MDMA, ibogaine, or ketamine, in line with prior research on subjective and community use features of psychedelics (Palitsky et al. 2024a).

text.text: Eligibility for the meditation arm was not limited to any prespecified set of practices or traditions, although these were assessed in the study measures.

Sample stratification targets were developed to support the recruitment of participants with ongoing AEs into the longitudinal study, such that n = 400 participants (50%) in each arm must have experienced <70% improvement in AE symptoms and have had their AEs onset within the past 12 months.

text.text: For the psychedelics arm, stratification targets also support adequate representation of different psychedelics, comprising at least 150 participants with AEs related to each: psilocybin, LSD, and MDMA.

Because of the existing use of ketamine in legal therapeutic settings, its occasional inclusion among psychedelics, and the corresponding need to assess its AEs, ketamine is included in this study; however, because the number of ketamine users may far exceed that of other psychedelics, the stratified sampling approach caps the number of individuals with ketamine-related AEs at n = 150 total.
Because other psychedelics (e.g., mescaline) are expected to be used less prevalently, no minimum sampling quota is set for AEs related to these substances.
Participants who fail validity checks or who appear not to be participating in good faith will be excluded.
These procedures are described below.
Participants will be recruited through several channels.

Direct outreach will be made to clinical and academic centers conducting clinical trials, asking them to share study flyers and information with participants who have completed their research studies.

Outreach will also be made to community organizations, advocacy networks, and educational entities, some of which provided formative input into the design of this study as part of community-engaged research.

These include peer support and special-interest organizations; organizations that support individuals experiencing recent or enduring psychedelic-and meditation-related AEs; and participants receiving psilocybin services at Oregon licensed psilocybin service centers, recruited with the support of community-engaged organizations informed about this study.
Further recruitment will occur through public appearances, lectures, and presentations (e.g., podcasts), as well as news bulletins from psychedelic-focused organizations (Palitsky et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Further recruitment will occur through public appearances, lectures, and presentations (e.g., podcasts), as well as news bulletins from psychedelic-focused organizations <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Palitsky et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In the case that recruitment milestones prove difficult to reach, paid targeted social media campaigns may be used for further recruitment.

Participants will be recruited from countries where psychedelic use has been decriminalized or legalized in any jurisdiction, pending country-specific approval by the Emory University IRB and international recruitment guidelines; current recruitment includes the United States, Canada, and Australia.
Recruitment is planned to continue for 36 months in order to reach adequate sample size and to account for attrition and rapidly changing access to psychedelics internationally.

Potential participants for each arm will complete a preliminary screening instrument specific to that arm, querying age, experience of psychedelic-or meditation-related AEs, and willingness to complete a follow-up live screening call.
Those who meet initial eligibility criteria will be invited to a live screening conducted over teleconference with study team researchers, typically 15 minutes in length.
In this screening, eligibility will be assessed through a set of open-ended questions aimed at discerning participants engaging in research in good faith from fraudulent participants.

These will take the form of a free-flowing conversation aimed at eliciting background information that would demonstrate lack of the kinds of experiences that would qualify a participant for this study.
These screenings will also provide opportunities to answer detailed questions about the study, offer transparency, and ensure that participants have a direct point of contact with the study team.

During study screenings, if participants have had AEs in the context of both meditation and psychedelics, they will be asked to identify one as primary (e.g., due to temporal precedence or subjective impact) and will be enrolled in the corresponding arm of the study.

In addition to live screening, survey data will be examined for indicators of nongenuine responding, including failed attention checks, internally inconsistent or impossible responses, implausible response times, and duplicate or automated submissions (Louis & Thompson, 2025; cf. verification procedures described in Ward et al., 2026).

text.text: Participants identified through these procedures will be contacted when feasible and excluded from analysis if their responses cannot be verified.
The baseline survey is expected to take approximately 90-120 minutes.
Participants may complete the baseline survey across more than one session, with responses retained and the survey required to be completed within 30 days of starting.

All participants will be sent up to three reminder emails and check-ins for each assessment in the study timeline if they have qualified for the study but have not yet begun to participate, or have begun an assessment but have not yet completed it.
Follow-up surveys for longitudinal study waves are expected to take approximately 30-60 minutes, with analogous completion windows and check-in procedures as the baseline survey.
Checks will be conducted weekly to identify participants meeting criteria for longitudinal follow-up (Participants).
Those participants will be contacted within one week and invited to participate in the longitudinal portion of the study.
Invitations will be sent to complete a followup survey two months after completion of the baseline survey, and every two months thereafter for one year.

Invitations to the voice diary component will be issued on a rolling basis to any participant in the psychedelics arm eligible for longitudinal assessment until all n = 40 diary participants are enrolled; these invitations will be made within the first week after baseline completion, with diaries beginning within two weeks of baseline completion.
Eligible participants will be compensated with a $30.00 gift card for the baseline survey.
Interviews will be compensated with an additional $40.00 gift card.

Participants who enroll in the longitudinal portion will be compensated at a progressively increasing rate for each completed assessment, beginning with a base compensation of $10.00 and increasing in increments of $3.00 for each successive wave (i.e., $10, $13, $16, $19, $22, and $25 respectively).
Weekly diary participants will be compensated $5.00 per diary entry, totaling $60.00 for 12 entries, with a $20.00 bonus for completing at least 80% of entries.

text.text: Use and practice history.
Participants in both arms report their lifetime history with the relevant practice; items are parallel across arms except where noted.
An open-ended item assesses age of first psychedelic use or first meditation practice.

Prior motivations are assessed via a 12-item checklist in each arm (e.g., "For social reasons (e.g., my friends were doing it)" in the psychedelic arm; "To gain insight into yourself or parts of your life/self-knowledge" in the meditation arm).

The prior psychedelic experiences is assessed via Likert-type items (never, once, 2-5 times, 6-10 times, 11-20 times, 21-50 times, 51-100 times, over 100 times) for each of: psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca, DMT (other than ayahuasca), peyote, mescaline (other than peyote), ketamine, MDMA, and ibogaine, with three open-ended "other" options.

Prior meditation experience is assessed by asking participants to indicate, from a list of 25 traditions including "no tradition," which they have practiced in, and from a list of 18 practice types (e.g., "observing the body (body scan)," "embodied movement practice", "contemplation of sacred texts"), which they have practiced at any point.
Participants are then asked to rank the types practiced from most to least, and report cumulative lifetime hours of practice.
An additional item asks whether participants have used wearable devices to assist their practice-whatever practice was specified.

Participants report the contexts in which they have engaged in the practice, using an 8-option checklist (e.g., "At a social event, party, rave, nightclub, festival, or concert", for the psychedelic arm; "In a meditation teacher training program", for the meditation arm; "On a multi-day retreat, for both") with an open-ended "other" option, and rank their endorsed contexts by frequency.

Participants who have attended multi-day retreats report how many they have attended and the duration of the longest; psychedelic-arm participants who took psychedelics as part of a spiritual tradition or retreat describe that tradition in an open-ended item.
To account for the existence of meditation and psychedelics co-use, both arms query ongoing and historic meditation practice and psychedelics use.

Responses to these items are used to narrow the options presented in the Agent, Set, and Setting Questionnaire below by means of survey logic, such that only previously-endorsed lifetime history responses are re-administered with reference to the index experience.
Agent, Set, and Setting Questionnaire.
A novel measure for the assessment of the agent, set, and setting at the time of onset of difficulties is included in the baseline questionnaire for both arms.

Questionnaire items were developed based on a review of prior literature (Aday et al., 2021; Aixalà, 2022; Breeksema et al., 2022; Carhart-Harris et al., 2018; Haijen et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2008; Perkins et al., 2021; Russ et al., 2019; Strassman, 2022).

text.text: Agent.
Items assessing the agent focus on the nature of the exposure associated with the onset of difficulties (the index experience).

In the psychedelic arm, participants indicate which psychedelic(s) they took prior to onset, using the response options presented in their use history; estimate how many times they had previously used that compound; specify the method of consumption; and estimate the dose ("Low dose (enough for you to feel a weak psychedelic effect)," "Moderate dose (enough for you to feel psychedelic effects)," "High dose (enough for you to feel extremely strong psychedelic effects)," or "Not sure"), with the option to specify an exact dose if known.
Further items ask how frequently they were taking psychedelics at the time, whether they were concurrently microdosing, and whether the index experience was precipitated by multiple doses.

In the meditation arm, participants indicate which of the 18 practice types they were engaged in at the time of onset and the amount of each (from "Very little" to "Very much"), and which was their primary practice, as well as which of the 25 traditions they were practicing in and which was primary, if any.
In addition, participants are queried about the typical daily meditation schedule they maintained at the time of the precipitating event; and, where a meditation app was used, its name.

The arms differ in one respect of consequence: in the meditation arm, difficulties need not arise from a single, datable index experience, and items accommodate onset that is gradual or cumulative across a period of practice.
In both arms, participants report use of other substances and prescription medications shortly before or during the index experience, including timeline and dosage.

Items assessing mindset at the time of the index experience comprise a 5-6 item questionnaire assessing preparatory behaviors, a 12-item checklist assessing participants' intentions for either psychedelics or meditation (e.g., to improve physical health, for social reasons, general self-improvement, to gain insight into oneself), and two sets of Likert-type items (1 = strongly disagree,7 = strongly agree) adapted from Perkins et al. (2021).

text.text: The first set includes 6 items querying mindset around the time of the experience (e.g., occurrence of a recent major stressor; preoccupation with other issues in life; sense of preparedness; mental and physical health; clarity of intention).

The second set includes 17 items querying mindset during the experience, assessing perceived control; acceptance or surrender versus resistance; redirection ability; and intense affective states such as fear, despair, and suffering.

Items assessing setting focus on the overall context of the experience (e.g., therapeutic program or therapy, spiritual or religious ceremony or practice, social event; retreat or group-practice context in the meditation arm), the social context (presence of a guide, leader, teacher, sitter, or other participants, the quality of interaction with them, and that person's expertise or professional role), the environmental context (e.g., safety, comfort, availability of support), the post-experience context (e.g., presence of integration), and additional supports available shortly before or after the experience (e.g., counseling, yoga, tai chi).

Items measuring the quality of relationships with others during the experience were adapted from established measures of therapeutic alliance: the Session Rating Scale (Duncan et al., 2003) and the Working Alliance Inventory (Horvath & Greenberg, 1989).

text.text: Influencing factors at onset of difficulties.

Additional factors surrounding the onset of difficulties, which are not properties of the agent, the participant's mindset, or the context of the experience, are assessed separately and include the following: Timing.

Participants report the recency of the index experience and, in the meditation arm, how recently difficulties began, how long after establishing a regular practice they emerged, whether they emerged within the first 50 hours of practice, and how long the daily schedule reported above had been maintained at the time of onset.
Health behaviors.
Participants in both arms report any changes in diet, food intake, or sleep patterns in the period leading up to the index experience.
Circumstances at onset.

Participants report their age and relationship status at the time of onset, whether they had children, and whether they were pregnant, had recently given birth, had recently miscarried or terminated a pregnancy, or were trying to conceive.
Assessment of symptoms and phenomenology: the CAPC and CAMC.

Symptoms and experiences that are part of the AEs are assessed using a novel item pool administered in two variants: the Comprehensive Assessment of Psychedelic-related Challenges (CAPC) and the Comprehensive Assessment of Meditation-related Challenges (CAMC).
The two variants comprise the same items, differing in instructions and wording that specify the psychedelic or meditation context.

To enable the development and validation of a measurement model from this pool, the CAPC/CAMC is described here as an assessment battery, containing a mixture of validated scales and individual items.

This item pool comprises 270 Likert-type items (1 = not at all,5 = extremely) designed to capture 59 previously-identified categories of symptoms and experiences across seven domains derived from qualitative research (Lindahl et al., 2017): cognitive, perceptual, affective, somatic, conative, sense of self, and social.
