text.text: It combines 261 items retained or adapted from existing measures, with 9 novel items developed for this study.

Items for all CAPC/CAMC scales were either generated in focus groups and/or interviews with meditators and/or psychedelic users with lived experience of enduring negative effects, or were adapted from preexisting scales.

Items were rated for inclusion or modification by meditator/psychedelic stakeholders, by researchers from multiple disciplines (religious studies, psychology, etc.), and by a psychometrician in a modified Delphi process (Fink et al., 1984) to yield the final set of items.

Influencing factors occurring after or in response to the onset of difficulties are assessed as follows.

Participants provide an open-ended narrative of their understanding of what caused the difficulties, followed by a checklist of explanatory frameworks they may have encountered from others: scientific or neuroscientific explanations; medical or psychiatric diagnostic explanations; spirituality and religion; trauma-related explanations; spiritual emergency (e.g., kundalini awakening); a normal part of the path or of spiritual progress; spiritual insight; purification (blockages, negative energy, sin, karma, evil spirits); incorrect practice or inappropriate psychedelic use; and preexisting psychiatric condition, plus two write-in options.

For each, participants indicate whether they encountered it and, if so, rate how often (1 = sometimes to3 = very often) and how helpful or harmful it was (-3 = extremely harmful to +3 = extremely helpful), with optional comments including who provided the explanation.

Participants report whether they disclosed their difficulties to others (e.g., partner, family, friends, community, healthcare professionals, teachers or guides, organizational leadership, "I didn't tell anyone," other), with optional comment, and rate the helpfulness of anyone they disclosed to (-3 to +3).

Psychedelic-arm participants are asked about psychedelic-specific coping actions (e.g., changing dose or compound, stopping use, reducing or increasing use, or repeating the same psychedelic experience unmodified or modified); meditation-arm participants are asked about contemplative coping strategies (e.g., attention regulation, acceptance or surrender, self-inquiry, reappraisal or application of views, stopping practice, reducing or increasing practice).

In addition, cross-arm use of remedies is assessed: psychedelic-arm participants are asked about contemplative coping strategies for post-psychedelic challenges, and meditation-arm participants are asked about psychedelic use for meditation-related challenges.

Participants report whether their difficulties are currently ongoing, how long their difficulties or symptoms lasted (ordinal,0 = ≤1 day to8 = >10 years), how recovered they currently feel (slider,0 = not at all recovered to100 = totally recovered), and how long they felt impaired as a result (0 = ≤1 day to8 = >10 years).

Where applicable, number of hospitalizations and total days hospitalized are queried.

Although self-report assessment of causality is imperfect, this study employs a series of questions across eight criteria designed to address some limitations of self-reported attribution and to evaluate the likelihood that reported experiences were causally related to psychedelics or meditation rather than to alternative causes (Britton et al., 2021; Lindahl et al., 2017).

text.text: Items query whether pre-existing conditions worsened after exposure; whether experiences occurred on more than one occasion; whether they lessened after stopping or decreasing exposure; whether they reappeared with resumption or increased exposure; whether the participant believes the experiences were caused in whole or in part by exposure; whether experiences first appeared during or following exposure; and whether plausible alternative causes could wholly account for the experience, with an optional openended description.
This variable additionally serves as a validity control: participants scoring below the cutoff for attribution of their AEs to psychedelics or meditation are excluded from analysis.
Qualitative and free-response items.
Open-response items appear at regular intervals throughout the sections described above, giving participants an opportunity to comment on any standardized assessment they have just completed.

At the end of the survey, participants are invited to submit their full account in writing, along with their understanding of why their experience occurred and which responses and remedies they found most and least helpful.
These responses support descriptive characterization and validity checking and may be subjected to content-analytic coding as part of a mixed-methods analytic strategy.

The longitudinal follow-up surveys, administered every two months (a total of six times) after completion of the baseline survey to participants endorsing ongoing difficulties, employ a subset of the baseline measures: the CAPC/CAMC and the WHODAS-II.

They additionally include the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (Zimet et al., 1988), comprising 12 Likert-type items (1 = very strongly disagree,7 = very strongly agree) assessing perceived support from significant others, family, and friends.

text.text: At alternating timepoints, participants complete different baseline sections: at 2, 6, and 12 months they complete the Remedies section, tailored to assess what remedies they have currently tried; at 4, 8, and 10 months they complete the Responses and Appraisals sections, tailored to track social responses received during the preceding period.
A subset of n = 40 participants is invited to complete a weekly assessment for 12 weeks.

Diary participants are purposely sampled from the longitudinal cohort on the basis of recency and persistence of difficulties: eligible participants report onset of their index experience within the previous six months and ongoing symptoms that are less than 70% resolved.
The assessment is administered via Fabla, a multimedia ecological momentary assessment platform (Arconada Alvarez et al., 2026 , Kaplan et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The assessment is administered via Fabla, a multimedia ecological momentary assessment platform (Arconada <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Alvarez et al., 2026</ref> <ref type="bibr">, Kaplan et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Participants receive a brief orientation and app training, including a practice survey and an opportunity to ask questions about the app or the items.
Weekly assessments are administered at 7-day intervals at a day and time of each participant's choosing (Fig 1).
text.formatted: Weekly assessments are administered at 7-day intervals at a day and time of each participant's choosing (Fig <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Each weekly survey remains open for 24 hours, with reminder push notifications delivered at 6-hour intervals until survey completion via Fabla.
Adherence is monitored by the research team, with two consecutive missed entries triggering a check-in call.
Each weekly survey takes approximately 10-15 minutes.
The first two items are voicerecorded prompts: "Thinking specifically about your [psychedelic or meditation] related challenges: how have things been going this week?"
and "Tell us, more generally, about your week."
Consistent with prior work using naturalistic narrative speech prompts (Kaplan et al., 2025), participants are instructed to "try to talk about this in a stream-of-conscious way for about 5 minutes.
text.formatted: Consistent with prior work using naturalistic narrative speech prompts <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Kaplan et al., 2025)</ref>, participants are instructed to "try to talk about this in a stream-of-conscious way for about 5 minutes.

text.text: Do not worry about pauses, stutters, or having the right things to say.
We are interested in hearing anything about this that comes to mind."
For both narrative diary items, an option to "type my response instead" is provided for participants who prefer to write rather than speak about their experience.

Participants then complete the IDAS-II Dysphoria and Well-Being scales (18 items), three items from the Sheehan Disability Scale (Sheehan, 1983) assessing functional impairment, with the total-work-days-lost item removed, and a single item assessing overall sleep quality (1 = terrible,10 = excellent).

Participants (n = 30 per arm; N = 60) representing a range of settings, symptom types, use contexts, and compounds, and including participants with both resolved and unresolved symptoms, are invited to participate in qualitative interviews.

Interviews use a semi-structured format to evaluate (1) phenomenology, (2) interpretive frameworks, (3) impacts, and (4) contributing factors, including coping strategies, elaborating on methods used by Lindahl et al. (2017) to study meditation-related AEs.

This protocol describes the study design, the core outcomes, and a defined set of initial descriptive and psychometric analyses, all of which will be preregistered as described in Open Science strategy.
Beyond data validation and preliminary descriptive characterization of the data, subsequent analyses will be independently pre-registered whenever possible.

The initial analyses comprise descriptive characterization of the sample and their difficulties, psychometric evaluation of the CAPC/CAMC batteries, description of functional impairment, thematic analysis of the qualitative and narrative data, and side-by-side description across arms.
These are the analyses the study will report first; they illustrate what the dataset supports rather than exhausting its analytic potential.
Analyses are to be conducted separately within each arm before any combined analysis.

Because psychedelic-and meditation-related AEs are expected to overlap, the effective sample available for evaluating a given item pool may exceed the n = 800 recruited into the corresponding arm; the extent of this overlap is not yet known, and will be reported descriptively.
Descriptive characterization.

Descriptive statistics will be reported for all study variables: sample composition; the compounds, practices, and contexts associated with onset; endorsement frequencies and severity distributions across the 59 categories comprising the batteries; duration, chronicity, and current status of difficulties; consequences and service utilization; and the remedies participants attempted with their rated helpfulness.

Remedy data are characterized descriptively, including whether the profile of remedies attempted differs by the characteristics, severity, or chronicity of difficulties; analyses treating remedies as predictors of outcome are deferred.
Structure of the CAPC/CAMC item pool.
Analyses specified at this stage of investigation will examine the structure of the CAPC/CAMC item pool.
Endorsement rates, variability, and inter-variable associations will be examined first.
Then, variables and standalone items showing minimal variability will be flagged and documented, rather than removed.

Exploratory factor analysis will then be conducted within each arm, with parallel analysis used to bound the number of factors retained alongside considerations of factor interpretability, followed by confirmatory factor analysis in a holdout sample.
Specification of rotation, estimation, and retention criteria will be documented in the pre-registration for this analysis.
Functional impairment.
WHODAS-II scores will be described by domain and in aggregate, within and across arms, together with the single-item overall functioning rating.
Associations between impairment and the characteristics of participants' difficulties will be reported descriptively.
Qualitative analyses.
Interview transcripts will be analyzed thematically and using an adaptive, inductive-deductive approach (Layder, 1998).
text.formatted: Interview transcripts will be analyzed thematically and using an adaptive, inductive-deductive approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Layder, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Diary narrative data are automatically transcribed using AWS transcription integration.

Transcripts will be checked and corrected as needed by a trained research assistant to verify accuracy, and will be analyzed using an adaptation of the structured tabular approach to thematic analysis for brief texts (Robinson, 2022), suited to the volume and brevity of weekly entries.
text.formatted: Transcripts will be checked and corrected as needed by a trained research assistant to verify accuracy, and will be analyzed using an adaptation of the structured tabular approach to thematic analysis for brief texts <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Robinson, 2022)</ref>, suited to the volume and brevity of weekly entries.

text.text: Narratives and detailed free-responses provided at various points throughout the cross-sectional and longitudinal survey forms may also be retained for thematic analyses.
Cross-arm description.

Symptom profiles, impairment, course, and remedy patterns will be described side by side across arms, providing the first empirical account of where psychedelic-and meditation-related difficulties converge and diverge.

Formal evaluation of whether measurement structures are parallel across arms, in the form of multigroup confirmatory factor analysis and tests of measurement invariance, is deferred, as it depends on the measurement model being established first.

Sample size was determined by the requirements of the full analytic program described in the Open Science strategy below, including analyses to be reported in subsequent registered reports, rather than by the initial analyses alone.
A sample of n = 800 per arm was selected to support the factor-analytic work described above.

Current standards suggest validation samples of at least 300 participants for each stage of exploratory and confirmatory analysis (Clark & Watson, 2019); n = 800 permits splitting each arm into training (n = 400) and testing (n = 400) sets while retaining adequate power in both after attrition.
text.formatted: Current standards suggest validation samples of at least 300 participants for each stage of exploratory and confirmatory analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Clark & Watson, 2019)</ref>; n = 800 permits splitting each arm into training (n = 400) and testing (n = 400) sets while retaining adequate power in both after attrition.

text.text: Power analysis for regression models indicates that n = 480 provides greater than 95% power to detect small effects (f² of .2).
Additionally, this sample size ensures adequate power to support possible future measure-development work, currently beyond the scope of this protocol.

For the longitudinal component, power was estimated through Monte Carlo simulation (Muthén & Muthén, 2002) using the R package simr, generating 500 samples of n = 240 to account for 40% attrition, with four repeated measures to account for 33% attrition.

text.text: Models were fitted using lme4 and included time, a longitudinal predictor, their interaction, a level-2 variable with a cross-level interaction, and three additional level-2 covariates, assuming random intercepts.
Simulations yielded greater than 95% power to detect an effect of .2.

The enriched longitudinal target of n = 400 per arm, with approximately 100 participants at each of 3, 6, 9, and 12 months since onset, was set to provide adequate representation across the range of compounds, practices, contexts, and symptom presentations expected among participants with recent and ongoing difficulties.

AEs can occur after both psychedelics and meditation, but their nature is not well understood clinically, hampering efforts to measure, prevent, and treat negative impacts.

Current detection paradigms underspecify subjective, SERT, perceptual, self-related, and interpersonal attributes, despite their reported importance to individuals with lived experience of AEs (Argyri et al., 2025; Palitsky et al., 2024a Palitsky et al., , 2024b)).
text.formatted: Current detection paradigms underspecify subjective, SERT, perceptual, self-related, and interpersonal attributes, despite their reported importance to individuals with lived experience of AEs <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Argyri et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Palitsky et al., 2024a</ref> <ref type="bibr">Palitsky et al., , 2024b))</ref>.

text.text: Thus, data that can support an empirically grounded, clinically useful understanding of AEs are needed.
This study addresses that need by generating a large, multi-method, longitudinal dataset characterizing these psychedelic-and meditationrelated AEs in detail.

Complementing qualitative work that has documented AEs falling outside standard clinical-trial detection paradigms (Lindahl et al., 2017; Argyri et al., 2025), it is designed to support the identification of clinically meaningful presentations of psychedelic-and meditation-related difficulties, examination of contributing factors, and detection of factors associated with improvement, persistence, or deterioration, analyses that will be reported in the pre-registered series described above.
text.formatted: Complementing qualitative work that has documented AEs falling outside standard clinical-trial detection paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Lindahl et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Argyri et al., 2025)</ref>, it is designed to support the identification of clinically meaningful presentations of psychedelic-and meditation-related difficulties, examination of contributing factors, and detection of factors associated with improvement, persistence, or deterioration, analyses that will be reported in the pre-registered series described above.

text.text: It further enables the examination of symptom cooccurrence patterns, which can allow for the detection of phenotypes related to psychedelic and meditation AEs, a goal that current AE dictionaries such as the CTC-AE_5 and MedDRA do not readily accommodate.

Difficulties following psychedelics and meditation are sometimes described as elements of an ultimately favorable trajectory, in which challenging experiences carry latent transformative benefits and ultimately yield improvement for those who experience them (Statharakos et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Difficulties following psychedelics and meditation are sometimes described as elements of an ultimately favorable trajectory, in which challenging experiences carry latent transformative benefits and ultimately yield improvement for those who experience them <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Statharakos et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This study will generate evidence bearing on trajectories that contribute to benefit as well as to harm, which can allow for an empirical test of the "it gets worse before it gets better" adage.

However, rather than categorizing difficulties into harmful or beneficial, the primary focus of this research is to bolster the development of frameworks for supporting individuals who experience AEs, providing care seekers and clinicians with evidence to reduce harm and to support recovery and growth.

The comparison of psychedelic-and meditation-related difficulties across the two arms may help clarify how deliberate practices and psychoactive compounds might differentially relate to subsets of AEs in what is otherwise an often-overlapping corpus (Palitsky et al., 2024b).

text.text: Nevertheless, the observational design precludes attributing differences to pharmacological action specifically.
A clearer account of convergence and divergence will support better detection and response in both contexts.
Several operational considerations bear on execution.
The principal challenge is recruiting and enriching the sample to meet the 50% target for recent and ongoing difficulties.
Although the study uses an enriched convenience sample, the varied legal status of psychedelics and the often-private nature of meditation practice may produce uneven recruitment rates between arms.

Identifying participants whose difficulties began within the past twelve months requires rigorous screening, as many individuals do not categorize their experiences as adverse until considerable time has passed.
The reliance on multiple digital platforms introduces specific considerations for data quality and retention.

Given the advertised compensation and an online survey ecosystem saturated with automated and disingenuous responding, the study implements live video screening calls with all prospective participants.
Participant burden is also substantial: the baseline survey is estimated at approximately 90-120 minutes.
Participants are invited to take breaks and resume at their convenience, and those who do not complete are contacted up to three times to identify barriers and provide reminders.
Longitudinal attrition presents a related risk.
With a twelve-month duration and six bimonthly follow-ups, the study is powered to withstand 40% attrition.

The team must nonetheless manage the possibility that participants with the highest levels of functional impairment may be the most likely to discontinue, which would bias longitudinal findings; this is partially addressed through personalized contact to identify barriers to completion.
Fabla's design has been purposely built to maintain engagement for long duration studies.
A virtual avatar, Fabio, acts as a companion throughout the study nudging and encouraging the participant to complete entries.
Preliminary evidence from multiple studies using the app supports that participants really like the avatar element, which paired with additional gamification elements aims to reduce study fatigue.
Additionally, the platform enables study coordinators to actively monitor participants and send push notification nudges if entries are being missed.
Lastly, a preliminary study comparing Fabla to a text-entry based EMA method found Fabla three times preferable over typed method (Kaplan et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Lastly, a preliminary study comparing Fabla to a text-entry based EMA method found Fabla three times preferable over typed method <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Kaplan et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Several limitations attend the design.

The first is self-report and retrospective bias: participants may not report accurately on current psychological phenomena (Paulhus & Vazire, 2007), and recollection is influenced by present experience (Ross, 1989).
text.formatted: The first is self-report and retrospective bias: participants may not report accurately on current psychological phenomena <ref type="bibr">(Paulhus & Vazire, 2007)</ref>, and recollection is influenced by present experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Ross, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal data collection somewhat reduces retrospective and recall bias, though self-report bias remains.
The second is the observational design: participants are not randomized, precluding causal inference.
The inclusion of a comparator arm helps distinguish effects associated with meditation from those associated with psychedelics, but does not establish causation.
Generalizability is limited linguistically and culturally.
Restriction to English-speaking participants in three countries limits inference to other cultural or global contexts in which these practices are common.
There is little evidence that the effects of psychedelics, or related AEs, are uniform across cultures, and such conclusions should not be drawn from these findings.
Moreover, the enriched sampling design of this study limits inferences about the prevalence of psychedelic-and meditation-related challenges at a population level.
Given this sampling strategy, it must be emphasized that participants cannot be taken as representative of psychedelic users or meditators in general.A final limitation is temporal scope.

Although one year exceeds the follow-up period of prior studies of psychedelic-or meditation-related challenges, and this study includes more longitudinal assessments than any to date, a one-year window nonetheless restricts interpretation at longer timescales.
Longer follow-up would be required to capture the full trajectory of enduring difficulties.
The principal risk is low enrollment or high attrition.

This is mitigated through a coordinated and flexible recruitment and retention strategy: all research partners contribute to recruitment, progress is monitored regularly, and compensation or procedures are adapted as needed.
Participants are clearly informed of study expectations, encouraged to commit to completion, and supported through reminders and follow-ups led by dedicated study personnel.

Recruitment is further strengthened by established networks in the psychedelic and contemplative research and practice communities and by structured compensation with bonuses for longitudinal completion.

The design accounts for moderate-to-high attrition, permits extension or targeted external recruitment if required, and places key measures early in the battery so that core data are retained even where completion is partial.
Ethical approval has been granted by the Emory University Institutional Review Board (#2025P011692).
All participants provide informed consent prior to enrollment.

Because the study involves reporting the use of substances that are currently illegal in several countries, the requirement for written documentation of consent has been waived, on the grounds that a signed consent document would constitute the principal record linking participants to the study and would therefore represent the primary risk of breach of confidentiality.
Identifiable information, including email addresses used for longitudinal follow-up, is stored on encrypted servers at Emory University and linked to survey data only via a study identifier.

Speech data collected via Fabla are securely and automatically transmitted through HTTPS requests to Emory University's Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)-eligible Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure.
Participants retain the ability to review their recordings via the app at all times, and can autonomously choose to delete past voice recordings from the app as well as from research records.
Recruiting a population characterized by distress or impairment requires careful ethical management.

The informed consent process and the initial video screening call are designed to give participants clear information and an opportunity to ask questions before beginning the survey, and to establish a direct point of contact with the study team.
Participants may skip any item, pause and resume the survey, or withdraw at any point without penalty.
At the time of writing, approximately 200 of the targeted 800 cross-sectional surveys have been completed in the psychedelic arm, and approximately 60 of the targeted 800 in the meditation arm.
Enrollment into the longitudinal follow-up is underway in both arms.
N = 9 interviews have been completed for the interview arm of the study.
As of the present writing (October 2026), no results have been generated, and no analyses have been undertaken.

Participant recruitment and data collection both began in summer 2025; recruitment is expected to be completed by the end of 2028, data collection is expected to be completed by the end of 2029, and initial results are expected by the end of 2028.

Results will be published in peer-reviewed journals and shared with participating communities, including the peer-support, advocacy, and educational organizations that contributed formative input to the study's design.
Given the community-engaged origins of several study components, findings will be returned to those communities in accessible formats rather than through academic publication alone.

Beyond the analyses reported by the study team, de-identified quantitative data and study materials will be made available to the broader research community under the tiered access model described above, so that other investigators may build on the dataset in future work on psychedelic-and meditation-related challenges.
Access to qualitative and audio data is more restricted, reflecting the re-identification risks these data carry.
Registered reports and pre-registrations arising from the study will be posted to the OSF repository as described above.

Example responses include active support, treatment as an important member of the community, being warned about risks, being blamed or shamed, being encouraged to view difficulties in spiritual terms, and being discouraged from taking medication.Remedies.

Participants report in an open-ended item what they found most unhelpful or harmful, then complete a checklist of attempted remedies: medications; vitamins and herbal supplements; non-prescribed psychoactive substances; psychotherapy; inpatient or residential care; complementary and alternative medicine; meditation or movement-based contemplative practices; psychedelic integration services; lifestyle changes (e.g., diet, exercise, sleep, changes in responsibilities); spiritually oriented resources or organizations; and named organizations (e.g., Cheetah House in the meditation arm).
For each endorsed remedy, participants rate how helpful they found it (-3 to +3).

Some remedy types elicit further questions: participants endorsing pharmacological treatment are asked which medications they tried; those endorsing complementary and alternative medicine are asked about specific modalities (e.g., acupuncture, energy work, traditional Chinese medicine, Ayurveda, naturopathy, homeopathy, chiropractic).
